2026. Last meeting: December 2, 2026. Location: Riley-Robb Hall B15.
Section: LEC 004 (to be confirmed).

**Instructor.** Prof. Ariel Ortiz-Bobea. Office: 450B Warren Hall.
Email: [ao332\@cornell.edu](mailto:ao332@cornell.edu){.email}. Office
phone: (607) 255-0220.

**Credit hours.** 3. Enrollment limited to AEM MPS students.

## Course description

AEM 6991 is the first half of the MPS capstone sequence. Over the
semester each team moves from a vague interest to a research plan that
can actually be executed in AEM 6992 in the spring. The deliverable is
that plan.

This section builds that plan in the order the work actually happens.
First, turn an interest into a question that can be answered. Then work
out **what evidence would answer it** --- which means commanding the
causal language applied economists use: counterfactuals and causal
graphs, what the standard models estimate, where uncertainty and
p-values come from, how inference goes wrong, and the designs that get
around each failure. Only then go looking for data, because the design
is what tells you which data you need. Teams who find data first end up
rationalizing a question around whatever they found, and that is the
most common way a capstone goes wrong.

The whole conceptual half is taught on examples from industry and the
news, before anyone opens a dataset. Then comes the part most capstones
skip: turning a construct into something a dataset can actually hold,
and the practical business of getting the data --- who holds it, what a
data-use agreement costs in months, what the IRB needs, and what
scraping and an API can and cannot get you. The back half is judgment:
what to ask of a dataset, driving an AI assistant to answer it,
checking whether the answer is credible, and seeing what a figure shows
and what it hides.

**Writing runs through the whole term rather than sitting at the end.**
The research problem is taught in meeting 2, the memo in meeting 10,
and the design paper in meeting 13, each with a short individual piece
attached. So does teamwork: the charter and the conflict protocol are
agreed in meeting 2, and every second session opens with a ten-minute
stand-up that is written down and graded. None of this assumes prior
econometrics or programming.

**This is not a coding course.** You will work with real data from
meeting 11 onward, and you will do it through an AI
assistant. What is graded is the questions you ask and the checks you
run --- never code you wrote. The reason is that writing the code is no
longer the scarce skill; knowing which analysis to ask for, and
noticing when the answer that comes back is wrong, is. Students who
want to build the pipeline themselves should take AEM 6850, which
teaches exactly that and cannot be compressed into three hours here.

## Audience and prerequisites

Open to, and required of, AEM MPS students. **No formal prerequisites:**
no econometrics, no prior programming, and none is taught. Where the
course touches data directly it does so through an AI assistant, so no
student is blocked by tooling. Students arriving with statistics or
coding experience will find the data work easy; the design vocabulary
and the verification habit will be new regardless of background.

## Learning outcomes

The registrar's outcomes for AEM 6991 are unchanged. By the end of the
semester students will be able to:

1.  **Teamwork.** Work effectively in small groups, complete tasks on
    time, and allocate work equitably among team members.
2.  **Problem focus.** Select and define a project problem that
    demonstrates relevant knowledge and articulates the significance of
    the problem.
3.  **Project design and workplan.** Develop a methodologically
    rigorous research design and identify key project tasks and
    outputs.
4.  **Presentation of progress.** Write about, present, and discuss the
    project in class with analytical rigor.

This section adds two outcomes that serve the four above:

5.  **Evidence sourcing.** Establish that the data a project needs
    exists, can be obtained on the project's timeline, and measures what
    the research question requires.
6.  **Design vocabulary.** State what identification strategy a project
    relies on, what it assumes, and what it therefore can and cannot
    claim.

## Software and tools

**There is nothing to install.** Everything runs in a browser.

-   One **AI assistant** that accepts file uploads --- Claude, ChatGPT,
    or Gemini. A free tier is sufficient.
-   A browser, and whatever you already write in.

That is the whole stack. Meetings 1--10 need no software at all.
Meetings 11--12 work on real data, and you will do that by uploading a
file to an assistant and interrogating it --- which is also how the
"do not upload restricted data" rule in the AI policy below stops being
abstract.

Scraping, APIs, and version control are covered at awareness level, in
meetings 10 and 13: what they are, what they cost, and when they are
worth it. You are not required to use any of them, and we write no
scrapers in this course.

## AI policy

Generative AI tools are **permitted by default** for all coursework.
Students are expected to use them, and to use them well. Three rules
apply to every deliverable:

1.  **Disclose what you used.** Every submitted deliverable carries a
    short disclosure block: which tools, on which parts of the work.
    The form is brief; what matters is that it exists.
2.  **Verify what the AI produced.** AI output is your work, exactly as
    code from a colleague would be. Two failure modes are graded
    against explicitly, because they are the ones that destroy a
    research proposal:
    -   **Fabricated citations.** Recent audits find invented
        references at high rates across leading models. Every reference
        in every submission must be one you have opened. A citation to
        a paper that does not exist is treated as a fabrication, not a
        typo.
    -   **Plausible-but-wrong design advice.** Models confidently
        recommend estimators whose assumptions your data violates. You
        are responsible for the design you propose.
3.  **Do not paste restricted data into a public chatbot.**
    Confidential, IRB-restricted, and proprietary data stay on your
    machine.

Failure to disclose is an academic integrity violation under the
Cornell Code. Failure to verify is graded against the rubric like any
other error.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Note.** Other sections of AEM 6991 restrict generative AI. This
section takes the opposite posture deliberately: the deliverable here is
a research proposal, which is precisely the genre where unverified AI
output does the most damage, and the skill worth teaching is
verification rather than abstinence.
:::

## Assessment

Half the grade is individual and half is team-based, so that no student
can be carried and no student is sunk by a team.

| Component | Weight | Type |
|:---|---:|:---|
| In-class quizzes | 10 % | Individual |
| Statement of interest | 5 % | Individual |
| Writing portfolio (4 pieces) | 10 % | Individual |
| Data exercises (2 × 5 %) | 10 % | Individual |
| Midterm | 15 % | Individual |
| *Individual subtotal* | *50 %* | |
| Team process | 10 % | Team-based, graded individually |
| Research problem presentation | 5 % | Team |
| Problem statement & literature review | 10 % | Team |
| Data feasibility memo | 5 % | Team |
| Research design paper | 15 % | Team |
| Final presentation & artifact | 5 % | Team |
| *Team subtotal* | *50 %* | |

Grading scale: A+ (≥ 98), A (≥ 92), A- (≥ 88), B+ (≥ 85), B (≥ 80),
B- (≥ 75), C+ (≥ 70), C (≥ 65), C- (≥ 60), D (≥ 50), F (\< 50).

### In-class quizzes (10 %)

One short quiz per meeting, delivered to your own device at 2:05, on
the assigned reading. Three to five questions, three minutes.

Many of them are scenario questions rather than definitions: *here is a
situation and a question --- which design fits, and what would have to
be true?*; *here is a design --- what would break it?*; *here is a
figure --- what is it hiding?*; *here is a step an AI just did for you
--- how would you check it without reading the code?* Those are the
questions worth asking, and they are the ones a chatbot cannot answer
for a student who was not paying attention.

The quizzes serve three purposes at once. They are the reading check
--- which is why this section does not assign Reading Notes. They are
the attendance record. And they surface confusion at 2:05, while there
are still two hours of class left to fix it.

Quizzes begin at meeting 2; there is no quiz in the first meeting.

**The lowest two quiz scores are dropped, and there are no make-ups.**
That covers illness, interviews, travel, and a dead laptop battery
without anybody having to email about it.

Quizzes are tied to your netid and timestamped. See *Data practices*
below.

### Statement of interest (5 %)

One to two pages, due before the second meeting. What you might want to
work on, why it matters, and what you would want out of it
professionally. Teams are formed from these, by the instructor.

Name **which of the five project archetypes** your idea would be --- and
why. The archetypes are introduced in meeting 1 and listed on that
meeting's page. Getting this wrong costs you nothing; not being able to
pick one at all is the useful signal, for you and for me, that the idea
is still a topic rather than a question.

### Writing portfolio (10 %)

Writing is taught in this course rather than assumed, and it is taught
as a method rather than as advice. A piece of writing is built outline
first: one topic sentence per paragraph, in order, before any prose
exists. The fastest way to learn that is backwards, so two of the four
pieces below are **reverse outlines** --- you take a finished text and
reconstruct the skeleton that must have produced it. Meeting 6 teaches
the method, meeting 10 applies it to the memo, and meeting 13 to the
design paper.

{{< include _writing.qmd >}}

These are graded on whether the argument survives contact with a
reader: is the claim in the first sentence, does the evidence support
it, and could somebody who is not in your team act on it. Length limits
are limits.

### Data exercises (10 %)

Two short individual exercises, 5 % each. They exist so that every student
personally handles data rather than delegating it to whoever on the
team seems most comfortable with it. Both are done with an AI
assistant, and neither is graded on code.

1.  **Interrogate a dataset.** Given a dataset you have not seen,
    submit the questions you asked of it, the answers you got, the
    checks you ran to confirm those answers, and the one thing you
    found that was wrong with it. Every dataset handed out has
    something wrong with it.
2.  **Rebuild and critique a figure.** Given a published figure and the
    data behind it, have the assistant rebuild it. Then produce the
    version you think is more honest, and say in three sentences what
    the original was hiding and whether it was hiding it on purpose.

What earns the marks is the interrogation and the verification --- a
correct output you cannot justify scores badly, and a wrong output you
caught yourself scores well.

### Midterm (15 %)

In class, first half of meeting 11. Open note, application-oriented short
answers. It tests whether you can apply the design vocabulary to
situations you have not seen --- not whether you memorized definitions.

### Team process (10 %)

The course description calls team leadership and management a major
component of this course, so it is graded as one rather than left to
goodwill.

- **The weekly stand-up.** Every session B opens with ten minutes:
  what you did since last week, what is blocked, and who does what
  next. It is written down and submitted with that session's output.
  The record is what makes an uneven division of labour visible in
  week 4 rather than week 13.
- **The charter.** Agreed in meeting 2, including the conflict
  protocol and how work is divided. You are graded on whether you
  actually followed it, not on how it reads.
- **Two peer evaluations**, in meetings 6 and 13, on a fixed template.

This component is team-based in subject and individual in grade: two
members of the same team can receive different marks for it, and
routinely will. A student who does not contribute does not receive the
team's grade.

### Team deliverables (40 %)

The sequence is the same one used across AEM 6991 sections, because it
is what AEM 6992 needs in January. **Nothing is submitted as a finished
paper out of nowhere.** Each written product is built in stages: the
**outline** first --- topic sentences only, in order --- then the
**sketch**, where each topic sentence gets its evidence in note form,
and only then the full text. Each stage is submitted and graded as part
of that deliverable's weight, so a broken argument is caught at the
outline, where fixing it costs an afternoon rather than a week.

{{< include _deliverables.qmd >}}

**The data feasibility memo is specific to this section.** It exists
because the most common way an MPS capstone fails is not a bad question
--- it is a good question whose data never arrives. Requiring the team
to prove the data is real while there is still time to change course is
the single highest-return deadline in the course. It is deliberately
placed after meeting 9 teaches you what to ask of a dataset and meeting
11 has you do it on real data --- you certify the data having actually
interrogated some, not from theory.

**Late policy.** Team deliverables lose 10 % up to 8 hours late, 50 %
from 8 to 72 hours, and are not accepted after 72 hours. Notify the
instructor before the deadline if something has gone wrong.

## Course schedule

Fourteen meetings. Each runs the same shape:

| Time | |
|:---|:---|
| 2:00--2:05 | Opening quiz on the reading |
| 2:05--3:15 | Session A --- the concept, on worked examples |
| 3:15--3:30 | Break |
| 3:30--3:35 | Second quiz on session A |
| 3:35--4:30 | Session B --- **your own project**, submitted before you leave |

Session B is not a lab exercise on someone else's data. It applies the
day's work to the team's actual project: conceptual clinics early in the
term --- draw your graph, name your design, work out what data it needs
--- and hands-on work once R arrives. The output is submitted the same
day. Fourteen of these, accumulated, are most of the research design
paper.

Every meeting has its own page, reachable from the sidebar, carrying the
readings, slides, and materials for that day. The table below, the front
page, and the sidebar are all generated from one file, so they cannot
disagree.

## Readings

Readings are assigned per meeting and posted on that meeting's page,
where the opening quiz is drawn from them. Everything assigned is free,
either through the Cornell library or openly online; there is no book to
buy. The full term list is settled in the first weeks and announced
here.

Two open texts carry most of Part II and are worth knowing about now:
Cunningham, *Causal Inference: The Mixtape*, and Huntington-Klein, *The
Effect*. Both are readable without prior econometrics, which is the
binding constraint in this course. Adams, Khan, Raeside & White (2007),
*Research Methods for Graduate Business and Social Science Students*
(SAGE), is the shared text across AEM 6991 sections and is free through
the Cornell library.

Recurring readings: Sandberg & Alvesson (2020) on problematization; Haas &
Mortensen (HBR) on teams; Stanley & Castles, *The So What Strategy*;
Zelazny, *Say It With Charts*.

## Attendance

The once-weekly format means missing one meeting is missing two
sessions. Attendance is recorded through the opening quiz and through
the session-B stand-up. Two dropped quiz scores absorb two full
absences without penalty and without a conversation. Beyond that,
missed quizzes score zero, and a stand-up you were not present for
cannot be filed retrospectively.

If you are going to miss more than two meetings, talk to me early
rather than late.

## Data practices

Quiz submissions are tied to your netid and timestamped, and are used
for grading and attendance. The roster, submissions, and any
per-student credentials are held in Cornell-managed or
instructor-controlled storage and are not published. Course materials
in the public repository never contain student-identifying data.

## Academic integrity

Every student is expected to abide by the Cornell University Code of
Academic Integrity. Work submitted for credit is your own. AI
assistance is permitted under the AI policy above; **failure to
disclose AI use is a violation**, as is submitting a fabricated
citation as a real one. Collaboration is expected on team assignments
and not permitted on individual ones.

## Accommodations

Students requesting academic accommodations should contact Cornell
Student Disability Services and give me their accommodation letter as
early in the semester as possible so arrangements can be made.

## Course materials

Slides, readings, assignment specifications, and the schedule live on
this site, which is generated from a public repository and updated
through the term. Canvas carries grades and submissions.
